questions.explanation: \(\tau_2 = C_{M2}(r_{o1}\parallel r_{oc1})\) (reader Eq. 15.11): both factors are big.

questions.prompt: Two identical, non-interacting stages each have a single pole at 10 MHz. What is the overall \(-3\ \mathrm{dB}\) frequency, in MHz?
questions.explanation: \(|H| = 1/(1 + f^2/f_p^2)\) reaches \(1/\sqrt2\) at \(f = f_p\sqrt{\sqrt2 - 1} = 6.44\ \mathrm{MHz}\). Equal poles stack up badly.
questions.figure_alt: Bode magnitude of two identical cascaded single-pole stages: flat at 0 dB, falling at 40 dB per decade above the shared pole frequency.

questions.prompt: How does inserting a source follower after stage 1 help the cascade's bandwidth?
options: Its low output resistance \(1/g_m\) drives stage 2's Miller capacitance, and its own \(C_{gs}\) is bootstrapped
It removes stage 2's Miller effect entirely
It raises the intermediate node's resistance
questions.explanation: The high-impedance node now sees only \(C_{db1} + C_{gd2}\) (reader Sec. 15.4.4).
questions.figure_alt: CS cascade with an internal source-follower buffer: node 1 (C_M1) at the input; node 2 with R_o1 and only C_db1 + C_gd2 (C_2); the follower (gain about 1) drives node 3 whose resistance is only 1/g_m2, loaded by the next stage's Miller capacitance C_M3; the last stage drives R_o3 and C_db.

questions.prompt: With the follower (\(g_{m2} = 2\ \mathrm{mS}\)) driving the next CS stage's Miller capacitance of 275 fF, find that node's time constant in ns.
questions.explanation: \(\tau_3 = C_{M3}/g_{m2} = 275\ \mathrm{fF}/2\ \mathrm{mS} = 0.1375\ \mathrm{ns}\) (Eq. 15.15), versus several ns without the buffer.
questions.figure_alt: CS cascade with an internal source-follower buffer: node 1 (C_M1) at the input; node 2 with R_o1 and only C_db1 + C_gd2 (C_2); the follower (gain about 1) drives node 3 whose resistance is only 1/g_m2, loaded by the next stage's Miller capacitance C_M3; the last stage drives R_o3 and C_db.

questions.prompt: Behind the follower, stage 1's output node (25 kΩ) now carries only \(C_{db1} + C_{gd2} = 10 + 5\ \mathrm{fF}\). Find its time constant in ns.

questions.prompt: Preview of amplifier compensation: why are several poles of similar magnitude dangerous once feedback is applied?
options: Their phase shifts add up quickly, eating the phase margin
questions.explanation: Each pole contributes up to 90° of lag; close poles reach 180° while the gain is still large.

Preview of op-amp frequency response: how do two-stage op-amps escape the cascade's closely spaced poles?
options: A compensation capacitor splits the poles, making one dominant and pushing the other out
By using equal poles on purpose
questions.explanation: Miller compensation across stage 2 deliberately exploits the Miller effect (pole splitting).
